entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10979"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.3.1-Ezek.3.27">Eze 3:1-27</reference>. Is Commissioned to Go to Them of the Captivity and Goes to Tel-abib by the Chebar: Again Beholds the Shekinah Glory: Is Told to Retire to His House, and Only Speak when God Opens His Mouth.</title> <div sID="gen19784" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10979"/><hi type="bold">1. eat ... and ... speak--</hi>God's messenger must first inwardly appropriate God's truth himself, before he "speaks" it to others (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.2.8">Eze 2:8</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10980"/><div sID="gen19785" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10980"/><hi type="bold">3. honey for sweetness--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.19.10">Psa 19:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.103">119:103</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.10.9">Re 10:9</reference>, where, as here in <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.14">Eze 3:14</reference>, the "sweetness" is followed by "bitterness." The former being due to the painful nature of the message; the latter because it was the Lord's service which he was engaged in; and his eating the roll and finding it sweet, implied that, divesting himself of carnal feeling, he made God's will his will, however painful the message that God might require him to announce. The fact that God would be glorified was his greatest pleasure. <div eID="gen19785" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10988"/><div sID="gen19794" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10988"/>12. (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.39">Ac 8:39</reference>). Ezekiel's abode heretofore had not been the most suitable for his work. He, therefore, is guided by the Spirit to Tel-Abib, the chief town of the Jewish colony of captives: there he sat on the ground, "the throne of the miserable" (<reference osisRef="Ezra.9.3">Ezr 9:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.1.1-Lam.1.3">La 1:1-3</reference>), seven days, the usual period for manifesting deep grief (<reference osisRef="Job.2.13">Job 2:13</reference>; see <reference osisRef="Ps.137.1">Psa 137:1</reference>), thus winning their confidence by sympathy in their sorrow. He is accompanied by the cherubim which had been manifested at Chebar (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.3">Eze 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.4">4</reference>), after their departure from Jerusalem. They now are heard moving with the "voice of a great rushing (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.2.2">Ac 2:2</reference>), saying, Blessed be the glory of the Lord from His place," that is, moving from the place in which it had been at Chebar, to accompany Ezekiel to his new destination (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.3">Eze 9:3</reference>); or, "from His place" may rather mean, in His place and manifested "from" it. Though God may seem to have forsaken His temple, He is still in it and will restore His people to it. His glory is "blessed," in opposition to those Jews who spoke evil of Him, as if He had been unjustly rigorous towards their nation [Calvin]. <div eID="gen19794" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10992"/><div sID="gen19800" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10992"/><hi type="bold">17. watchman--</hi>Ezekiel alone, among the prophets, is called a "watchman," not merely to sympathize, but to give timely warning of danger to his people where none was suspected. Habakkuk (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">Ha 2:1</reference>) speaks of standing upon his "watch," but it was only in order to be on the lookout for the manifestation of God's power (so <reference osisRef="Isa.52.8">Is 52:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">62:6</reference>); not as Ezekiel, to act as a watchman to others. <div eID="gen19800" type="x-p"/>

Men are not to flatter themselves that their ignorance, owing to the negligence of their teachers, will save them (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.12">Ro 2:12</reference>, "As many as have sinned without law, shall also perish without law"). <div eID="gen19803" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10994"/><div sID="gen19804" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10994"/><hi type="bold">19. wickedness ... wicked way--</hi>internal wickedness of heart, and external of the life, respectively.<div eID="gen19804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19805" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">delivered thy soul--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">Is 49:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.26">Ac 20:26</reference>). <div eID="gen19805" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10995"/><div sID="gen19806" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10995"/><hi type="bold">20. righteous ... turn from ... righteousness--</hi>not one "righteous" as to the root and spirit of regeneration (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.33">Psa 89:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.138.8">138:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.12">Is 26:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.3">27:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.28">Joh 10:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.6">Php 1:6</reference>), but as to its outward appearance and performances. So the "righteous" (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.17">Pr 18:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.9.13">Mt 9:13</reference>). As in <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.19">Eze 3:19</reference> the minister is required to lead the wicked to good, so in <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.20">Eze 3:20</reference> he is to confirm the well-disposed in their duty.<div eID="gen19806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19807" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commit iniquity--</hi>that is, give himself up wholly to it (<reference osisRef="1John.3.8">1Jo 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.3.9">9</reference>), for even the best often fall, but not wilfully and habitually.<div eID="gen19807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19808" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I lay a stumbling-block--</hi>not that God tempts to sin (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.13">Jas 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.14">14</reference>), but God gives men over to judicial blindness, and to their own corruptions (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.16">Psa 9:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.9.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.94.23">94:23</reference>) when they "like not to retain God in their knowledge" (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.24">Ro 1:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.26">26</reference>); just as, on the contrary, God makes "the way of the righteous plain" (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.11">Pr 4:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.15.19">15:19</reference>), so that they do "not stumble." Calvin refers "stumbling-block" not to the guilt, but to its punishment; "I bring ruin on him." The former is best. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10998"/><div sID="gen19813" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10998"/><hi type="bold">24. set me upon my feet--</hi>having been previously prostrate and unable to rise until raised by the divine power.<div eID="gen19813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19814" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shut thyself within ... house--</hi>implying that in the work he had to do, he must look for no sympathy from man but must be often alone with God and draw his strength from Him [Fairbairn]. "Do not go out of thy house till I reveal the future to thee by signs and words," which God does in the following chapters, down to the eleventh. Thus a representation was given of the city shut up by siege [Grotius]. Thereby God proved the obedience of His servant, and Ezekiel showed the reality of His call by proceeding, not through rash impulse, but by the directions of God [Calvin]. <div eID="gen19814" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10999"/><div sID="gen19815" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10999"/><hi type="bold">25. put bands upon thee--</hi>not literally, but spiritually, the binding, depressing influence which their rebellious conduct would exert on his spirit. Their perversity, like bands, would repress his freedom in preaching; as in <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.12">2Co 6:12</reference>, Paul calls himself "straitened" because his teaching did not find easy access to them. Or else, it is said to console the prophet for being shut up; if thou wert now at once to announce God's message, they would rush on thee and bind them with "bands" [Calvin]. <div eID="gen19815" type="x-p"/>
